Difficile de réaliser que cette expérience se termine ! Dune a pompé toute ma joie, toute mon énergie tel un vers des sables. La seule chose notablement plaisante dans ce très long-métrage est ses plans : très jolis, beaux à voir. Bien que les costumes notamment bellement réalisés permettent de se projeter dans cet univers alternatif de fiction qu'est Dune . Malgré tout, ce film fut une torture et m'a renvoyé au jour qui avait déterminé le début de ma longue période de haine envers le cinéma. Sa lenteur, son écriture, son essence n'a pas grand chose à envier à Twilight , surtout au niveau du personnage principal. Pourtant, je suis surprise de le voir reconnu de façon différente que celui-ci ! Finalement, je préfère oublier cette expérience horriblement ennuyeuse (et ennuyante) — même si cela me sera difficile.

I tried watching this once before and gave up like 12 minutes in because I was confused and bored. Turns out I just needed to let the movie cook. The world building here is fucking insane. I loved the politics between the different houses and how each one has its own identity, while Paul’s destiny slowly develops in the background. The movie doesn’t rush to explain everything either; it lets you be confused sometimes and gives you the answers later. I’m especially interested in seeing what Paul becomes because you can already feel how much potential and power he has. But I wasn’t nearly as invested in most of the characters. Besides Paul, Jessica and Chani, a lot of them felt disposable. Duncan was one of the few supporting characters I actually liked and then they got rid of him way too easily. Some of the dialogue also felt forced, especially when Paul started saying some of the weirder shit. Production-wise though, holy shit. The production design is insane. The ships, architecture, costumes and scale make this universe actually feel massive. Villeneuve’s wide shots aren’t just there to look pretty either; Arrakis and the desert tell you things about this world without anyone having to say a word. The large-scale scenes are incredible, the sound design is powerful, and even though some effects like the shields could’ve looked better, visually this movie is ridiculous. And Hans Zimmer… this would genuinely be a different movie without him. The score gives so much power to the world and makes the slower pace work incredibly well. It’s definitely slow, but once I understood that this is the beginning of a much bigger story, I stopped caring about the runtime. Instead of finishing it bored like I expected, I finished it curious as fuck to see where this story and Paul go next.

Villeneuve signe la mort du blockbuster Quelle perte de temps ... Encore une fois la moyenne de Senscritique me sidère. Je conçois qu'il fait partie de ces films tant attendus, attendu comme le saint graal dont même l'immense Lynch s'est vautré (pour des raisons facilement explicables). Mais le niveau de nullité de l'adaptation de Villeneuve est astronomique. Impersonnel, plat, aseptisé, anesthésiant, j'en ai marre de ces films standardisés qui n'ont aucune singularité, je mets ma main à couper que la version de Lynch est plus intéressante. D'abord notons que vouloir esthétiser des décors aussi uniformes, on parle quand même d'une diégèse se déroulant constamment sur le sable, est particulièrement laborieux mais pas impossible, pourvu que le réal se creuse un peu les méninges. Hélas Villeneuve rend ses décors complètement stériles, impalpables, sensation renforcée par le numérique qui rend le tout d'une morosité soporifique. Et pourtant Villeneuve est loin d'être le dernier des abrutis puisqu'il s'en est plutôt bien servi pour Blade Runner 2049, jouant sur le faste, le chatoyant, des contrastes de couleur collant parfaitement à l'univers avant-gardiste, or Dune lui n'exhale rien, c'est la définition même du vide. Notons que cet esthétisme va aussi désamorcer les feux d'artifice, les guerres qui font l'effet d'un pétard mouillé. Villeneuve a carrément massacré son ver géant qui est tout sauf géant, il n'effraye personne, car non seulement l'esthétisme ne le met à aucun moment en avant, faute à une luminosité faible et l'arrivée de la nuit, je plissais des yeux pour essayer de voir un pixel de la bête, mais le jeu des grandeurs ne va pas jusqu'au bout, plutôt que d'avoir une caméra à hauteur d'homme constante, on l'évince rapidement pour garder une vue aérienne de la bête. Même Skyline, qui est un immense navet, était plus impressionnant sur cet aspect, offrant quelques contre-plongées en intro et à la fin pour ensuite cloitrer ses personnages dans leur appartement de bourgeois étasunien et les laisser contempler la catastrophe, il s'agit d'un navet qui a coûté 10 million de dollars, Dune a coûté 165 million, où se cache la supercherie ? Est-ce les acteurs qui ont empoché le pactole ? Venons-en à ces acteurs qui ne cessent de m'horripiler : un grand gaillard dont on se fout complètement, de toute façon Villeneuve scelle son destin sans aucun suspens. Un petit jeunot incarnant l'archétype du faiblard destiné à de grandes choses et qui doit se forger pour mieux s'affirmer. Une petite starlette issue de la mode qui s'est dit un jour que le cinéma l'érigerait parmi les plus grands, mais n'a que son faciès univoque de petite minable pontifiante je-sais-tout et je-vous-emmerde-tous pour offrir au spectateur. À titre de comparaison, Kitano, qui dans tous ses films n'a aucune expression, a une palette d'émotion exorbitante. Kitano n'a aucun talent d'acteur et pourtant il fracasse toute la clique de ces misérables histrions frivoles adulés par des êtres qui ont un besoin immédiat d'identification. On s'identifie aux personnages qui nous représentent spirituellement. Dans Dune les personnages sont des marionnettes, des objets mécaniques archétypaux à l'esprit annihilé qui ne représentent rien. Zendaya est présenté comme un personnage secondaire et qui pourtant, introduite dans les réminiscences éminentes de Chalamet, la hisse parmi les plus importants de par son aspect "symbolique" (j'insiste sur les guillemets), à partir de là on devine déjà les prémices d'une relation amoureuse complètement bidon qui sera développée dans le second opus, mais déjà nous avons les fameux bégayements, regard éperdu. Nous avons souvent hué Lynch dans la mise en scène des combats extrêmement kitsch, mais qu'on ne vienne pas me faire croire que chez Villeneuve c'est mieux, c'est tout aussi ringard et inefficient, je dirais même que ça produit l'effet inverse. Déjà le montage surcoupé maladroitement dessert les combats, mais en plus nous ressortons de la salle sans comprendre vraiment la particularité de ces combinaisons protectrices. D'ailleurs ça permet de rebondir sur un autre problème inhérent au genre, ceux qui déploient des gadgets, des concepts surhumains détruisent les limites qui permettent de garder une forme de tangibilité à l'univers, sinon ça laisse place à de multiples deus ex machina : personnage principal qui peut contrôler un individu par la parole, pouvoir lire dans le futur ... Ensuite il faut absolument évoquer la volonté d'intensifier les enjeux mais qui ont l'effet inverse escompté. Le coup du ver géant qui se réveille parce que nos deux personnages ont marché sur du sable tambour c'est ridicule. Faut-il produire un décret pour condamner tous les artistes qui relancent les enjeux par le biais d'artifices prévisibles et pathétiques ? Likewise, no story — let alone the misshapen first half of one — could ever hope to support the enormity of what Villeneuve tries to build over the course of these interminable 155 minutes (someone mentions that time is measured differently on Arrakis), or the sheer weight of the self-serious portent that he pounds into every shot. For all of Villeneuve’s awe-inducing vision, he loses sight of why Frank Herbert’s foundational sci-fi opus is worthy of this epic spectacle in the first place. Such are the pitfalls of making a movie so large that not even its director can see around the sets. How big is “Dune”? We’re talkin’ slabs upon slabs of angular concrete as far as the eye can see, spaceships that seem to displace entire oceans when they emerge from the seabeds of Caladan, and sandworms so large they could eat the Graboids from “Tremors” like bar nuts. Even yoked kings Jason Momoa and Dave Bautista look like tabletop miniatures when placed against its backdrops, as if cinematographer Greig Fraser discovered a way to shoot deep focus and tilt-shift at the same time. So why, for all of its unparalleled immensity, does watching “Dune” amount to the cinematic equivalent of being handed a novelty-sized check made out for six dollars? Why is the scope of Villeneuve’s dream betrayed by the dull shallowness of its reality to the point that his film’s most astounding effects — which are every bit as tactile and transportive as those in “Blade Runner 2049” — feel more like optical illusions? The biggest problem, though, is Hans Zimmer, whose score is incredibly loud and unremittingly the dominant sound for more of the movie’s 155 minutes than not. Zimmer’s approach to musical cultural appropriation has been blithe since at least 1994’s The Lion King , while his subsequent rise to Coachella fame has accelerated improbably. Both worlds collide in Dune ’s score, a nightmare barrage of field-filling drums punctuated by the odd muezzin-ish call to prayer—given how fraught the material already is (brown-skinned desert peoples vs. The Man), the Orientalist tinting is poorly thought through. Every time I went to the multiplex in summer 2016, I’d walk past an auditorium booming the thunderous punching-sounds foleys and Zimmer’s score from Batman v. Superman: Dawn of Justice , and it never failed to make my life a little more unpleasant. Longer review/ramblings coming very soon. ---------------------------------------------------------------------- Dune may, in the end, prove to be unfilmable after all. Frank Herbert’s vision was one of such an epic scope that it just doesn’t seem to find a right fit in the cinematic medium. Villeneuve however tries his very, very best to fit it in there no matter what. He creates a universe so grand that it barely fits the cinema screen. One scene with unimaginably big spaceships gets put to shame by the next scene with even bigger spaceships. Spaceships the size of planets move about the universe to carry this epic story and yet, for all that stupendous spectacle, Dune feels painfully hollow. Villeneuve wants to take his sweet time to ease us into this complex saga and does so formidably at certain points, but he also gets caught up in the uncontrollable scale of it all to such a degree that the human factor almost crumbles under the weight of the story’s grandeur. The all-star cast is scrambled through the film like a joke, with some actors popping up for only a few minutes to deliver a faint impression of what their character wants and needs. Chalamet’s Paul Atreides serves perhaps the only worthwhile character arc that has some weight to it while most of the people swarming around him leave a faint impression at best. Their frail, human existence simply cannot live up to the immensity of Arrakis or the universe at large. Villeneuve lost his grasp when trying to combine the epic with the intimate and only got a little bit of both without realizing how to combine the two and make them add up to each other. And still, as much as this film is overshadowed by its epic nature, those moments are in hindsight, as flat as all the rest of it. Spectacular, grand imagery with nothing to say other than: “This is big. This is huge!” The Villeneuve-fanbase has clearly already deemed this a masterpiece despite having had zero chance to see this with a critical eye but I could bet on my life that what will stay with them about this won’t be the story but simply the visual spectacle. And Dune is so much more than that. It’s a human spectacle that happens to play on a massive scale but even with Villeneuve’s plan to split this in two to give everything its supposed bit of gravitas, Dune (part one) falls painfully short. At best it’s an oversized prologue, filled with exposition both in its dialogue and in its imagery to prepare you for the (hopefully) more in-depth approach of the second part.

"Dune" de sciencefiction-evenknie noemen van "Lord of the Rings" is vloeken in de donkere kamer. "Dune" is een verhaal over goed en kwaad, episode 10191. Weer een film over opstanden tegen de gevestigde orde. De mooie mensen zijn de goeden, de lelijke zijn de slechten. De kritiek op kolonialisme en ecologisme ligt er zo dik op, dat het oninteressant wordt. En het politieke steekspel tussen de verschillende huizen is al zo dikwijls uitgepuurd dat het cliché wordt. Dit bombastisch woestijnepos is veel te complex en absoluut niet duidelijk. Waar gaat dit verhaal naartoe? De vroegere versie uit 1984 van David Lynch was een miskleun, maar dit lijkt me evengoed een peperdure, overhypte flop! Ook de cast redt het niet in deze technologische onzin. Echt onder de indruk van de personages word je niet, ook al worden ze vertolkt door acteurs/actrices met naam. Chalamet kan het niet recht trekken. Brolin, Momoa en Bardem zijn geweldige namen, maar worden veel te weinig in beeld gebracht om boeiend te zijn. Ook de muziek van Hans Zimmer is bombastisch en luid, maar vooral storend. De kijker wordt serieus onderschat: hoe dikwijls moeten we Pauls dromen zien om te weten dat Zendaya een belangrijke rol gaat spelen in zijn leven? Dat heb je al door na 1 maal. De beelden laten je achter met een gevoel dat je dit al zo dikwijls gezien hebt (en het langdradig wordt). De spanningsboog zakt gewoon in elkaar op het einde, een einde dat je achterlaat met "oef, gedaan" en niet met een verlangen naar meer. De film is gebouwd op drijfzand en zakt er onvermijdelijk in.

Mixed feelings about Dune. It's clearly an epic, larger than life film in almost every sense of those words. Strong cast, and cinematography/visuals; it intrigues from the very start by throwing audiences right into this fantasy/future world, and I really like being thrust into a story rather than get everything spoonfed to me at the start of a movie. But I did feel frustrated at times, and that frustration is mostly with the script and the fact that Dune does not trust its audience--sometimes not even to remember stuff they showed 30 minutes ago. Aside from its very beginning, it spells everything out for you in the dialogue/Paul's dream sequences. I understand there has to be exposition, especially in a story as big as this, but viewers can piece things together themselves! After showing something, you don't need to follow up with an immediate line explaining the very thing you just saw . But despite my reservations, Dune looked incredible enough to make me interested in the next part.

"Guardare Dune in televisione è come guidare un motoscafo nella vasca da bagno. Per me è ridicolo. È un film che è stato realizzato come tributo all'esperienza del grande schermo". Da questa dichiarazione di Villeneuve mi sento di trarre due polemiche: 1) Un regista che paragona la visione del proprio film a un giro su un motoscafo non è degno di essere considerato un Maestro del cinema contemporaneo. E infatti Villeneuve non lo è, benché moltissimi pretendano di insegnarci che lo sia. Tuttavia ha ragione, guardare Dune è come guidare un motoscafo: può divertire nel mentre, ma quando l'esperienza finisce non rimane nulla. Non si esce dalla sala cambiati nello spirito. Ci rifletta chi parla di Villeneuve come di un grande artista. 2) Basta differire, è giunto il momento di inveire contro la retorica dell'"esperienza del grande schermo": se il tuo film ha bisogno di uno schermo enorme e di un mirabile impianto audio per poter essere apprezzato, significa che è un brutto film. O meglio, non è un film: è un giro in giostra. O su un motoscafo. I capolavori restano tali che li si guardi su un grande schermo o su un cellulare. La questione è importante, perché se ci si convince che per salvare il cinema si debba salvare "la sala" si fa confusione tra un'arte e uno dei luoghi che può accoglierla. Per come la vedo io Dune visto al cinema è spettacolo, Amour visto su un televisore è cinema. Per salvare il cinema bisogna in qualche modo incoraggiare la produzione e la distribuzione di film in cui si esprima lo sguardo unico e insostituibile del proprio autore. Se non si faranno più film come Amour , il cinema sarà morto. Se non si faranno più film come Dune , ci resterà sempre il motoscafo. Tutto ciò sia inteso non come una critica a Villeneuve, che si diverte, guadagna un sacco di soldi e viene pure chiamato Maestro!, quanto a chi - critici, riviste, blog - fa passare continuamente prodotti commerciali per arte. Si parla di Villeneuve come del Maestro che coniuga abilmente "autorialità" e "intrattenimento" senza rendersi conto che dove ci sono enormi budget e mille persone coinvolte nei processi decisionali che conducono al film non c'è spazio per l'espressione della personalità del regista. Che infatti in Dune non c'è: è un blockbuster come un altro, girato e montato con un ritmo un po' più compassato affinché si possano ammirare le duecento, insignificanti inquadrature-cartolina e a fine visione ci si senta in diritto di pronunciare una delle più orrende frasi di moda di questi tempi (insieme a "è girato bene"): "Bella la fotografia!". Cito un Maestro vero, Bresson, che nei suoi appunti annotava: "Nessuna bella immagine!". Una confessione: mi piace il reggaeton. Ma non mi sognerei mai di affermare che il reggaeton è arte. Non è musica. Quei brani sono commercialate che scimmiottano il linguaggio - chiamiamolo così - di Bach. Mi domando perché chi apprezza le commercialate che scimmiottano il linguaggio cinematografico spesso si infiammi quando gli si fa notare che film come Dune stanno al cinema come Bailando sta alla musica. Perché si fa fatica ad accettare serenamente che possano piacerci le cafonate e a chiamarle col loro nome? Sul film in sé, quattro parole: fredda sequela di cliché. P.S. (sennò pare che odi Villeneuve): i suoi primi film mi piacciono, La donna che canta in particolare. La sensazione è che poi il regista sia stato gradualmente assorbito dal sistema hollywoodiano fino a diventare un pigro fabbricatore di cartoline. P.P.S: leggo oggi queste parole del nostro: "Se parliamo della Marvel, il fatto è che tutti questi film sono fatti con lo stampino. Alcuni registi possono aggiungere un po’ di colore, ma sono tutti della stessa fabbrica. Non toglie nulla ai film, ma sono formattati. Dune è estremamente personale". E poi: "Ho cercato di rendere possibile il film più popolare. Un film per tutti [...]. Ho pensato al pubblico giovane, ho aperto le finestre; Ho cercato di essere mainstream". I film estremamente personali non vengono concepiti cercando di essere mainstream né pensando a quale pubblico rivolgersi. È un'evidente contraddizione. Poi possono anche piacere a tutti e diventare enormi successi (anzi, sono convinto che se i film personali ricevessero la stessa distribuzione dei film commerciali le persone smetterebbero di guardare questi ultimi), ma di certo non vengono scritti e girati con l'obiettivo di piacere a qualcuno.

First of all, disregard all the five-star reviews, there's no way even for the biggest Dune or Villeneuve fan to seriously think this movie is a masterpiece other than to hype up their fellow fans ahead of the release (a commendable action that makes for a nevertheless dishonest rating) Talking about the movie: there's no way around it, it's pretty bland and forgettable. Almost all of its problems come from its meandering pacing—full of useless things while glossing over a lot of important and/or interesting ones that would have improved the movie—which I think comes from Villeneuve's desire to faithfully adapt the parts of the novel he likes the most clashing with its cinematic potential as a whole: e.g. we don't even see House Atreides space-travelling to Arrakis, although the movie tells us right at the beginning that the reason because the Spice—the very thing Dune revolves around—is "the most precious substance in the universe" is precisely that's so essential to space travel. Worry not, however, because we get to see instead Jessica choosing her housemaids in Arrakeen 😎😎😎 (This is to introduce the Shadout Mapes, a character from the novel which in this movie serves no purpose whatsoever other than being… a character from the novel, and makes her only other ten-second appearance later and dies) And so on, and so on... I have to say however that the faithfulness also makes for a good thing: in the 1984 adaptation, the part in the desert after Paul and Jessica escape was greatly reduced, becoming boring and uneventful, while here is not only more fleshed out, but it is straight up the best and most enjoyable section of the movie, with the flying chase scenes being almost Mad-Maxian (*high* praise right here!). It alone makes you almost wish for a sequel Black marks: Hans Zimmer's score is AWFUL and annoying to the point of effectively distracting you from what's happening on screen at times (which wasn't already that captivating on its own), the fight scenes are somehow even clumsier than the old ones, and—well—that's it: as I said before, it's just really mediocre.

This was, undeniably, epic. But not in the way Herbert probably intended. Villeneuve's Dune is told from a whole other perspective than the book. It stems from a mind craving action-packed sequences and technical grandeur, a mind keen to please a public eye trained by the likes of the MCU. Attempting to amalgamate that mindset with Herbert's text, which makes a point of avoiding wordy descriptions of fights and focusing instead on the power play and the political machinations, is all but doomed to fail. Villeneuve expands upon technicalities that Herbert skipped and instead either leaves out or dumbs down the complex net of suspicion, betrayal, loyalty, and plotting that Herbert so delicately weaved throughout his book. The result is a huge cast of characters with little to no believable intention and charm, a set of beautiful cardboard people if you will, riding fleets of various intricately designed huge vehicles and looking over incredibly vast and glorious landscapes. A feast for the eyes, but hardly more than that. It may well be that Dune is unadaptable for the big screen, probably even the small screen. So much of this book's story goes on solely in the minds of the characters and hardly ever has anything on a screen of any size managed to deal with the proper communication of an abundance of thoughts. However, when faced with that obstacle, Villeneuve does not try his hand at rising above it. He runs the other way, shifting the storyline's focus instead to the action sequences and the machinery. His film, therefore, works more as a mere visual companion to the book rather than an adaptation.

This new incarnation of Spice World is essentially Game of Thrones in space, and threatens at every other moment to collapse under the considerable weight of its own self importance. There are impressive vistas to behold, sure, but the storytelling is leaden, and the overly heavy usage of slow motion certainly does not help alleviate the sluggish pace. Neither does Hans Zimmer's ethno-screechy soundtrack attempts at moving things along, by mostly amping up the volume and wailing to give an illusion of intensity. That said, Denis Villenueve's ultraformalist style of filmmaking is never without surface level riches - his movies look (and mostly) and sound impressive, and so it is with this adaptation of the first half of the Dune novel too. But beyond that this had little to offer me. At 2.5 hours you really need to provide more substance than this, but it doesn't, and I was mostly bored and unengaged for the duration of it. A final, technical note: I saw this in IMAX, and the constant aspect ratio changes drove me nuts. Filmmakers, if you're going to shoot in IMAX format, fucking *commit* to it! Dune , one of the most anticipated films of this year. Partly because of Frank Herbert's influential book it is based on, partly because this may finally be the adaptation everyone's been waiting for after the first attempt . Although I think Villeneuve's version surpasses its predecessor, I can't help but feel a sort of emptiness after watching it, where I hoped it would be awe-inspiring and linger in my mind days afterwards. There are several things at work that contribute to the best and worst of this sci-fi epic, which is only the first half of Herbert's first book. This choice helps to give the story more time to develop over the course of its two-and-a-half hours, but also stretches the events out to a point where it loses its pace. The moment in the story where Part I finds its conclusion is logical, but happens quite sometime after its peak, wherefore the last half hour or so feels too much as an outstretched epilogue. About the casting choices: As much as all the actors seem to be born for their role – they all perfectly fit the description; in this film and according to the book – I couldn't help but see them apart from their other roles. That's the danger with such an all-famous cast as this. Whenever Gurney (Josh Brolin) spoke, I heard Marvel's Thanos. When Leto (Oscar Isaac) talked about wanting to be a pilot, I thought about Poe Dameron from Star Wars. Only Dave Bautista and Rebecca Ferguson seemed to accomplish totally transforming themselves in their role. That actually brings me to another point: How much this doesn't feel like a whole new world with its own rules and vibe; something that Herbert's book certainly is. Somehow, it feels too earthy. Instead of taking me to a galaxy far, far away, the oriental vibe only brought me to another place on Earth. The various space ships, costumes and interiors (wonderfully designed; I'm not gonna lie about that) seem to be the only things reminding me this is science-fiction. In any case, it needed a little more mystique, something that's only really accomplished in the 'fear-scene' where Charlotte Rampling asks Timothée Chalamet to put his hand in the box, and the famous words "Fear is the mind-killer. Fear is the little death that brings total obliteration" first get spoken. I admire Denis Villeneuve for being able to get such a vast and complex story off the ground, and, despite my critique, I really enjoyed it. There are multiple moments that got me really excited. But, I keep thinking about how much more creative, mystique and off-worldly this could be. Lynch's version may not be a success, but it has all of this what Villeneuve's hasn't, and is therefore closer to my heart. Of course, this is a new vision that shouldn't be blindly compared to the other, but considering the hype and Villeneuve's reputation, it's a bit of a letdown. Ranked: Denis Villeneuve - 2021 Crossed off: Hyped 2021

Peut être que le film était trop attendu ? Peut être que le défi était tout simplement impossible à relever avec brio ? Toujours est-il que je suis sorti déçu du cinéma ce soir. Denis Villeneuve, à qui l’on doit Premier Contact, film plein d’intelligence et d’idées visuelles fortes et originales, nous amène tout un plateau de préjugés hollywoodiens fades et redondants. Tout d’abord, l’histoire : Paul Atréides est l’Élu galactique qui veut sauver les peuples opprimés. Il comprend son rôle d’Élu en ayant des visions de l’avenir. L’histoire se passe sur une planète désertique, sur laquelle évolue un Vers de sable géant… autant de déjà vus. Soit, l’histoire n’est pas de Villeneuve, puisqu’il s’agit d’une adaptation de roman. Pour autant, la mise en scène n’a rien d’original non plus : là où la planète désertique aurait pu offrir de sublimes lumières, on se retrouve la moitié du temps plongé dans une demi pénombre d’où aucune lumière ne sait émerger avec grandeur. D’ailleurs, ce désert ressemble trait pour trait à celui de Star Wars Rogue One. En allant dans ce sens, les costumes ont l’air tout droit sortis d’une penderie de chez LucasFilm; et si un ou deux vaisseaux ont des design atypiques et plutôt réussis au début du film, on se retrouve vite à cours de bonnes idées. Les antagonistes - en bon méchants qu’ils sont - évoluent dans des décors sombres, ont des voix bien trop graves pour être réalistes, et respirent très fort. Une bonne idée survient tout de même à la fin du film : le bain noirâtre du Baron, qui intrigue tant par sa couleur que par sa texture. Bien qu’anecdotique, ce détail détonne tellement dans le champ visuel qu’il nous fait prendre conscience d’un défaut majeur du film : il manque de texture. Les décors en intérieurs sont tous beaucoup trop épurés pour être réalistes, et la peau des personnages (même ceux vivant dans le désert) est tellement lisse que ça en devient ridicule. En un mot : l’univers de Dune, tel que représente par Villeneuve, n’a pas de vie. Quelle déception également de voir Hans Zimmer au générique ! C’est donc lui qui nous a pondu des basses vrombissantes vues et revues pendant les scènes d’action, à la seule originalité d’une cornemuse trop discrète ? Ajoutez à cela un jeu pas toujours juste de Timothée Chalamet, et vous avez de quoi décevoir toute la population d’un salon de SF en un seul film… Pour autant, je ne me suis pas ennuyé durant les 2h30 (tout de même…) que dure ce périple galactique. Sans avoir été pris spécialement en haleine, j’ai été facilement et efficacement immergé dans l’univers Dune, dont on m’avait pourtant dit qu’il était complexe. En somme, c’est un bon divertissement hollywoodiens, comme tout un chacun a déjà du en voir une vingtaine. Quelques bonnes idées disparates, des plans assez jolis, un sound design très bien ficelé, et le tour est joué. Mais je pense qu’il faut être difficile avec ce film. Très attendu, il n’a fait qu’être un divertissement de plus qui permettra, dans 5 ans, de faire passer un dimanche pluvieux. C’est sans doute de là que provient la plus grande déception : on ne veut pas voir l’univers de Dune traité de la même manière aseptisée et stéréotypée que Star Wars, les Gardiens de la Galaxy, et toutes la ribambelle de licences qui s’en suit. Pour conclure, je ne sais pas si Denis Villeneuve a échoué à adapter Dune au cinéma. Il n’empêche qu’il a fait un film quelconque là où Franck Herbert, avec son roman, avait su modifier en profondeur la face de la SF.

I really wanted to love Dune, but I didn't. Throughout the entire runtime I was waiting for one scene to hook me, to engage me in what's happening and allow me to immerse myself in the experience. But it never happened. For full transparency's sake, I read the book earlier this year and saw the Lynch film shortly after, so I went in knowing full well what the plot was and how another film adaptation handled the material. And while Lynch's Dune is riddled with problems in its pacing and plotting, there are things it suceeds in over Villeneuves latest endeavor. But we'll get there when we get there. The biggest problem in this newest adaptation of Herbert's seminal work is Villeneuves incessent gigantomania. When he said this film needs to be seen on a big screen, he was right, but I don't think any screen in the world will be able to make the size of this film look manageable. Every starship in this film is the biggest it can possibly be, Arrakeen, the capital of Arrakis, is an amalgamation of absolutely massive concrete buildings built almost on top of each other and the armies standing in formation seem endlessly big. Because everything is the enourmous size it is, none of it ever feels believable. When the courtyard of your palace is a massive concrete plain that stretches as far as the eye can see, but is entirely devoid of any markings, wells, walkways or any signs of life, they just look like computer-generated textures. When the ships are all huge grey blocks with no discernible characteristics or features, they just become big blocks that look artificially placed in an empty-looking environment. Dune is big because it is filled with literally huge structures and buildings and ships, but they never feel organic. Which is the next big issue. None of the sets the characters inhabit feel lived-in, or natural, or like they convey an actual world. Why Villeneuve opted for every building to be a grey slab with grey walls and nothing on them, I cannot for the life of me understand. None of its feels alive, vibrant, or remotely natural. It's all just copy-pasted textures that have nothing to them. Contrast this with Lynchs version and the lush round and gold features on the palace exterior and interiors, the beautiful ornaments and art-deco-looking elements. They have character to them, and they give a sense of personality to the area the characters are inhabiting. Villeneuves environments feel dead by comparison. Speaking of dead: To call the characters lifeless would be an overstatement, however, they do all have an air of imposed seriousness on drabness to them, that weighs down on the general atmosphere a lot. Never is there a sense of levity, of a character being content, and actually tender moments between characters are very sparse. The only actor that is allowed to have the slightest charisma is Jason Momoa, but even then he does not get the opportunity to let it shine much. Timothée is good at what he does, though he always looks like he's constipated. The rest of the cast has to abide by the general tone of the film, which is unflinchingly serious, to a fault. Again, Lynch was able to incorporate genuinely touvhing moments while condensing more story into less runtime, so why couldn't Villeneuve? All of these elements, the artifical scale, the lifeless set design, the one-note characters, it all leads to a very distant and cold experience. Never did I ever emotionally engage in anything onscreen, the film started and then it ended and I was left pretty unphased by everything. It's such a shame, because the book as well as Lynchs film both have spectacle and scale as well as emotion and very human moments. But Villeneuves Dune could have also taken place on an ice planet and it would have fit the tone of the film almost better. The main difference between the two films is that the newer really wants to take it's time and properly tell the story of Frank Herberts Dune. While Lynchs film tries to tell the entire story in two hours, essentially crippling it and leaving an overstuffed mess, the new Dune is intent on staying true to the details of what Herberts Dune is about. Except for the fact that there is still a lot missing. Not just details and single exchangeable scenes, but actual plot threads that fans liked (I know I'm not the only one upset over the plot line about the investigation into who the traitor is missing). So this new Dune is longer than the old one, and only tells half the story, but because the plot is decelerated so much the 150 mins feel like 240. The first hour of this film drags for very long, since exposition in reading is easier to digest than exposition in film, especially when in film it is just delivered through dialogue. At the same time, so much happens in this first movie already, that thinking about having to go see another one like this feels like a chore. It still feels overstuffed. Overall, this is definitely the better adaptation of the book Dune, though it is not finished yet. The second part is going to be far more interesting than the first, so I'm keeping my hopes up. In conclusion, while conceptually more mature and structured better than previous iterations, Villeneuves first Dune film can't help but bury its great base material under heaps of comically oversized imagery (Hans Zimmers oppressive and incredibly loud score only makes this film heavier and clunkier), an atmosphere that is way to stern and self-important for its own good and an approach to its base material that is taking its time, which has two sides, as it allows for more detail and clearer themes, but at the same time still seems like its barely managing to hit all the story beats before credits roll. This Dune needed more refining in a lot of places, and overall, its not bad. It's just not as good as everyone wanted it to be. I don't want to seem like I hated this film, so here are a list of things I liked: The cinematography largely supported the narrative quite well (though also succumbing to the aforementioned gigantomania) and generally looked pretty good. The CGI is entirely seemless (except for the artifical building exteriors and interiors). Everyone in the cast is sexy as fuck. The story of Dune is finally getting a worthy adaptation, though it is a flawed one. Might see this Dune again soon, might change my mind.

I remember back in the days, after the first few Game of Thrones seasons came out, I thought that this show was quite bloated, filled with unnecessary filler and a story that would probably work better as a movie series à la The Lord of the Rings . Eventually tho, I started to realize that there might be more to it and when I finally read the books between seasons 6 and 7, my previous assumption did a complete 180. The show wasn’t bloated, it was rather a condensed version of an even more detailed book series, books that explained a lot of the things I didn’t get in the show, because there they were only mentioned briefly or left out entirely. I retroactively developed a completely new appreciation for the show .. until season 7 came around, but I digress. The point is, when Dune was announced, I immediately wondered, given my previous experience, whether it would be useful to read the books first this time, but I still didn’t end up doing it. The main arguments being: a) It’s written and directed by one of the most accomplished filmmakers of our time. He will make it work. b) A movie is supposed/designed to work on its own anyway. c) I simply didn’t want to spoil myself knowing the story beforehand, possibly robbing myself of some amazing cinema experience and d) I didn’t assume Dune could be anywhere as complex as Game of Thrones . Well, after having seen the film, I totally wished I had read the books, at least the first one. The movie has to establish a whole new sci-fi world with all its rules and features and Villeneuve does in fact invest quite some time to setup persons, cultures, beliefs, ideologies, items and a whole lot of other things that seem to carry a lot of weight for the characters, yet I still felt like I’m missing something to fully grasp why this world is how it is and why the people are how they are. As a result, I could never fully connect to the movie and therefore I didn’t really care all too much about anything or anyone. It was almost ironic that when I finally started to become invested into the story .. it was over. If Dune: Part 2 will get made, it might retroactively clarify a thing or two that didn’t reveal themselves to me in this movie alone, but the solution to all my problems might simply be to just read the books. I’m quite certain this movie will grow on me either way. For now tho, I’m just not really feeling it.

他，回來了！Denis Villeneuve用熟悉的「慢條斯理」，來處理這份難以搞定的佳餚，手法幹練卻不失細膩之處，以一個沒看過小說的視角帶入，確實有難以消化的難處，但本片不至於像諾蘭那樣具有「干擾性」，而是可以輕易地貼近角色來了解架構的「引導」，然而，本片的弱點，也正是因受到原著及商業類型的束縛，導致成品流露出虛假與流於表面，最終成為另一部虎頭蛇尾的鉅作。題外話，如果你真要體驗到本片的壯觀，拜託去IMAX或ATMOS廳體驗，那種震撼與感動交織而成的「屏息」，難以形容。 《沙丘》算是維勒納夫中段班的作品，或許是因為有改編難度的壓力，整體看上來還是綁手綁腳的，不像《異星入境》與《銀翼殺手2049》那樣「放得開」，但他的導戲功力已達頂峰，大場面的調度讓人驚嘆連連，龐大的世界觀他也能處理得毫無匠氣、游刃有餘，從沙漠瀰漫的危險感，到室內空間的窒息感，都能捕捉到其深刻之處。劇情基本遊走在殖民與天選之子上，然而，劇本的空泛台詞與過度簡化，多少還是影響了兩個主題的力度，裡頭的傳承與戰勝恐懼的意象，則因為情節的不穩定，與兒戲般的轉折，讓這象徵意義變得薄弱，只剩「說出來」的表面意義。 說實話，如果沒了這群演員的表現，本片的角色塑造絕對會崩塌，裡頭我最愛Rebecca Ferguson的演出，她將眼淚化為角色的痛苦展現，母性的光輝清晰可見，隱忍與噴發的情緒拿捏得宜。漢斯季默，宛如為電影戴上一層淒美的面紗、穿上悲壯的戰衣，人聲總是能帶出電影最唯美的一面，可惜配樂的編排使整體情緒過滿，導致配樂干擾了劇情進行與情緒延展，人聲則因為頻繁的出現，給人煩躁的印象。聲音設計著實令人難忘，爆炸與打鬥的聲音富有層次感，衝擊力更是做得恰到好處，可惜，高亢配樂的過度氾濫，讓音效展現不了真正的實力。 《沙丘》在我看來，就是部相當適合大銀幕的作品，場面調度無懈可擊、音效特效傑出無比，創造出一場宛如《星際大戰》的視聽享受，可惜這場史詩，敗在劇情的單薄，支撐不了片長與大場面的輸出，《魔戒》之所以能支撐得了三個小時的打磨，就是因為劇本的可塑性及魅力，才能讓情緒持續延展下去，但《沙丘》犯了一個錯誤，就是用過多的篇幅來「介紹」，及彆扭的角色塑造，使電影少了收放自如的情緒，及大小場面切換的流利，更少了角色之間激盪的火花。 但這個缺點，仍無法改變本片是商業巨作的事實，Denis Villeneuve用極為藝術與富有情調的氛圍，讓影片既有沙漠的粗曠，也有人性的細緻，這，正是維勒納夫電影之所以吸引人的所在。然而，這只是《沙丘》的第一篇章而已，接下來，還有許多寶藏等著維勒納夫來挖掘，希望這告一段落的時間，能讓Villeneuve適應商業片的呈現。最後，一顆星給場景設計及特效的絕美，一顆星給眾星雲集的卡司，一顆星給Denis Villeneuve純熟的導戲功力。

Το «Dune» του Ντενί Βιλνέβ, βασισμένο σε έναν φανταστικό κόσμο του μέλλοντος, όπου ισχυροί οίκοι οικογενειών εξουσιάζουν ολόκληρους πλανήτες ενώ το πιο πολύτιμο υλικό που υπάρχει είναι ένα πανάκριβο μπαχαρικό που επιτρέπει την διαπλανητική μετακίνηση, είναι πλέον εδώ: γυαλιστερό, πιστό στο πρωτότυπο υλικό, γεμάτο τάσεις μεγαλείου και μια αυθεντική αγάπη για όλα όσα αγκαλιάζει αυτό το σύμπαν, σε μια ευλαβική σχεδόν προσέγγιση. Αλλωστε ο Βιλνέβ είχε ήδη αποδείξει τις ικανότητες του και στην εικονογραφία της επιστημονικής φαντασίας («Αφιξη», «Blade Runner 2049») αλλά και στο χτίσιμο μελλοντολογικών, πολύχρωμων ή μη, κόσμων. Η ματιά του ήταν ανέκαθεν επική, η αφήγησή του πάντα έβρισκε τον άνθρωπο ανάμεσα σε όλα τα τεχνολογικά επιτεύγματα και τα κάδρα του μόνιμα αρέσκονταν στο να ανακαλύπτουν νέους τρόπους να δει κανείς τον κόσμο. Στο «Dune» ο Βιλνέβ επιμένει στα δυνατά του στοιχεία, ρίχνει φως στις ερήμους του Αράκις και τα παλάτια των Ατρειδών, βουτάει στο σκοτάδι των Χαρκόνεν και τα οράματα του Πολ με την μυστηριώδη Τσάνι που υπόσχεται μια ακόμα πιο μεσσιανική συνέχεια και παρουσιάζει κάθε χαρακτήρα με στόμφο και βαρύτητα, χορογραφώντας τις κινήσεις τους με αυστηρότητα και ντύνοντας τα λόγια τους με υφέρπουσα τραγικότητα, κλείνοντας το μάτι στην αρχαία ελληνική τραγωδία που έτσι κι αλλιώς επηρέασε (όχι μόνο λόγω «Ατρειδών») το έργο του Χέρμπερτ. Το μόνο που θα μπορούσε κανείς να προσάψει στον Βιλνέβ είναι το γεγονός ότι δεν τολμάει να ρισκάρει ή να προχωρήσει σε αιρετικές επιλογές, τουλάχιστον προς το παρόν. Από την άλλη όμως, ακριβώς αυτό είναι και το δυνατότερο σημείο της ταινίας: ένα «Dune» φτιαγμένο για τους οπαδούς του «Dune» και ένα δώρο σε όλους τους φαν που εδώ και δεκαετίες ανέμεναν μια εντυπωσιακή και επική κινηματογραφική μεταφορά αυτού του κόσμου. Και όπως λέει η Τσάνι της Ζεντάγια «Αυτό είναι μόνο η αρχή.» Πληρης κριτική της ταινίας από το 78ο Φεστιβάλ Κινηματογράφου της Βενετίας, στο Flix.

Venezia 78 #1 Dopo anni di spasmodica attesa, un posticipo doloroso ed una distribuzione controversa, Dune di Denis Villeneuve comincia a mostrarsi al pubblico e alla critica, suscitando reazioni più miste di quanto auspicabile. Vedo di iniziare con uno spirito più positivo per non dare idee sbagliate su ciò che effettivamente penso del film : è un’opera mastodontica, che spinge i limiti di ciò che può essere messo in scena in un contesto fantascientifico, che suscita un sense of wonder tolkeniano anche nei suoi momenti più bui e tenebrosi, introduce concetti accattivanti e stimolanti, utili a ribaltare la superficie già vista e già conosciuta dei ruoli e dei percorsi dei vari personaggi, portati in vita da performance sublimi e stratificate, anche se alcune sono più sprecate di altre. Però non posso fare a meno di chiedermi il perché di alcune decisioni editoriali di scioccante ingenuità da parte del regista e dello studio, che lasciano il film fondamentalmente incompleto, un eccitante inizio di un percorso che si rischia di non vedere mai. E questo inizio è davvero immenso, travolgente e a tratti inebriante nella sua immersività scenica e nella sua mitologia pregna di politica, filosofia, spiritualità e misticismi vari, ma commette il peccato originale di qualsiasi blockbuster, ovvero quello del non reggersi interamente sulle sue spalle e sprecare il suo terzo atto in promesse che rischia di non poter mantenere… 2 anni e mezzo dopo, un rewatch in sala e a due settimane dalla Parte Due, mi sento solo di chiedere umilmente scusa a Denis. Monumentale inizio, non vedo l’ora di vedere la monumentale conclusione.

The moment passed as swiftly as it came, but it's emblematic of a movie that almost buckles under the weight of its own worldbuilding as well as setup for things to come. Almost, I say, because it doesn't succumb completely, instead coming out on top to deliver an experience that thrills as well as awes, even in spite of its stumbling blocks. In that, it's not quite Blade Runner 2049, Denis Villeneuve's masterwork, but it's also far grander than that film, in scope as well as ambition. With Dune, there is a lot of ground to cover. The book has often been said to be "unfilmable", and it's easy to see why: its world is vast, its factions numerous, and its story incredibly dense. Because of this, the movie - billed as "Part One" on its opening title screen - only covers the first half of the book, opting to leave the latter half to a promised sequel. That's a gamble, because Dune spends so much time setting up its world and conflicts that if this doesn't get a follow-up, it would be infinitely frustrating: by the time the credits roll, the story's far from over. In many ways it feels like we're just getting started. This is where Dune will almost certainly divide people. Some may feel it's too much setup and not enough payoff; especially in the first half, viewers may experience the same thing I did in the aforementioned scene, to momentarily be taken out of it as they try to process this new influx of information. There's also the chance that people will feel disappointed by the end of the film, because it hinges a lot of itself on the promise of more to come: Zendaya, for instance, doesn't get all that much to do here, and the climax might be smaller-scale than some are hoping (though it really works on a narrative level). That's not to say the worldbuilding and setup are bad or unnecessary, in fact quite the opposite: there's just a lot of it. However, where Dune stumbles through these narrative shallows, if you allow it to find its footing as the sweeping political saga that it is - "Game of Thrones in space" as it's often called, though that comparison only applies insofar as it's about noble houses vying for control in a game of courtly intrigue, backstabbing, and all-out war - it absolutely wows, not just on a story level, but also visually as well as auditory. Rolling dunes, spaceships falling out of orbit, spice flowing through the air and sandworms filling the screen... its world of Arrakis and the noble houses of Atreides and Harkonnen are beautifully put to screen and sound, with a grandness to them that one so rarely finds in cinema anymore. The score by Hans Zimmer is terrific and cinematographer Greig Fraser has a beautiful eye on where to put the camera. The cast, too, gives it a Shakespearean feel: among others Oscar Isaac, Rebecca Ferguson, Stellan Skarsgård (in terrific make-up), and especially Timothée Chalamet and Zendaya (when she's in it) grace the screen beautifully. With this film it's clear that Villeneuve isn't afraid to give everything from its actors to its towering spacecrafts, to the grains of sand on Arrakis the attention they deserve. Looking back on the film now, a few days after I've seen it, I am strongly reminded of those history classes when the teacher starts telling a story, and at first you're not sure where it's going and there's a lot of information being thrown at you, but by the time the bell rings you're so invested that you don't want to leave, and you cannot wait for the next class - or, in this case, movie. I just hope Villeneuve gets to make it.

Nothing can prepare you for the grand-scale epic Denis Villeneuve has in store with this instant science fiction classic, and perhaps the best first entry in a franchise since ‘The Fellowship of the Ring’ and ‘The Matrix’. Although interpreting well-known themes of environmentalism, totalitarianism and religion, that have been seen explored hundreds of times on screen since the release of Frank Herbert’s influential novel, everything feels new through the masterful lens of Villeneuve (working for the first time with great DoP Greg Fraser). The story succeeds where ‘Blade Runner 2049’ failed, simply because it is allowed time to develop organically and be fully fleshed out. Sure, there is exposition, but all information is to the point. Villeneuve focuses on spacecrafts in motion, the specificities of the different planets and the movements and bodies of the main characters, all of which seem fully formed from the get go. The result is a riveting spectacle unmatched by current Hollywood filmmaking. The worldbuilding is extraordinary, rivaling ‘Game of Thrones’ when it was still at its best. Villeneuve’s mastery is apparent from the decision to focus more on the complex power plays at hand, rather than indulge in unnecessary set pieces. This makes it all the more effecting once everything goes to shit, with some of Villeneuve’s best suspense scenes since ‘Sicario’. Timothée Chalamet is great in the lead, but Oscar Isaac really blew my mind with his deepfelt performance. From this to ‘The Card Counter’, he has solidified his position as one of the most interesting actors working right now. Please go see this on the biggest screen possible (Also Zimmer's pitchperfect score demands the loudest speakers possible). This is the kind of film that brings hope to blockbuster filmmaking. And sadly, it is not automatically guaranteed high gross and renewal like other blockbusters of this day and age (I am looking at you ‘Fast and the Furious’). Yes, I am hyped. Welcome aboard.

78th Venice Film Festival - #4 „Dreams are calls from the deep.“ After two years of waiting and nearly unbearable hype, after having read the first book and finding myself in the middle of the fourth at the time the movie premiered, I am in a difficult position where it's nearly impossible for me to distinguish between DUNE as a movie and as an adaptation. My temporal solution is to not even pretend being objective and write down my first spoiler-free impressions. DUNE feels grand. What often is nothing more than a common catchphrase used for blockbuster cinema is put to the extreme here; the scale of the movie feels so large it's nearly terrifying, when monolithian ships darken the sky, whole structures vanish into the void of a sandworm or Baron Harkonnen is floating through rooms like a looming shadow. Additionally, the movie often plunges into very dark imagery - ritual sacrifices, mass executions - that make Star Wars (to set this stupid comparison aside right away) feel like a toy advertisement. All of this is accompanied by the best score Hans Zimmer has composed in years, pieces that range from hauntingly beautiful choire sections to nightmarish soundscapes that will literally send shivers down your spine. The atmosphere created by all of this is truly alien; apart from the planets surfaces, everything looks, feels and sounds out of this world, what is, paradoxically, a feat few Sci-Fi-movies achieve. Long story short: The technical perfection put to display is awe inspiring at every minute. When faced with a world as rich and complex as Herbert's universe, Villeneuve had to decide on which aspects to focus and he clearly chose worldbuilding above all else, which may be frustrating for those who expect emotionally charged, character-driven conflicts, but is a feast for people who enjoy similarly getting lost in the cultural and historical lore of, for example, Tolkien's Middle-Earth. Book readers, above all else, will be more than pleased to see that even smallest details made it into the movie, littering every set and backdrop. DUNE constantly introduces, shows and explains new weapons, vocabulary, traditions, locations and characters - sometimes elegantly and with ease, in rare cases a bit on the nose. Same goes for the script, that most of the time achieves condensing large world-spanning conflicts into emotional dialogue but in a few scenes struggles with relatable character development during plot-defining moments. The cast is phenomenal though; Timothée Chalamet and Rebecca Ferguson giving the best performances by far, followed by the undeniable presence of Oscar Isaac’s father figure, who, despite having few scenes, connects exceptionally well on an emotional level with his son and the audience. The upper mentioned rough edges, little dents and imperfections end up not even feeling like weaknesses because nearly every criticism on that level can be traced back to an uncompromised faithfulness to the novel, that make DUNE a less streamlined blockbuster at the same time as it makes it a much better adaptation. That’s why we see just the beginning of the main battle scene and then immediately cut back to Paul or why a movie with so little time for all its content spends a few minutes on a gardener explaining the water situation on the planet instead of something that would create more plot advancement. Whenever possible, atmosphere is chosen over conventional dramaturgy, exposition is chosen over character study - and then it all suddenly ends. That ending surely is the elephant in the room when speaking about DUNE. The last scene is basically a teaser for the second part of the story, while the first one ends without a climax or relief and yes, that’s incredibly frustrating but at the same time very much intentional. The movie serves as a introduction into a world that feels unique, captivating and truly immersive. It sets the groundwork for interesting characters whose developments have barely been initiated. It gets you invested in large conflicts and plots that remain unresolved. And it’s downright perfect in all of that. I left the cinema speechless, shaking and slightly disappointed. Speechless because DUNE Part One is a movie I thought could not exist in our current blockbuster cinema. An untamed, uncompromised creative vision with an enormous budget from a director whose last movie was a financial failure. I was shaking because I have never been as immersed in and overwhelmed by a fictional world put on screen since I saw the Lord of the Rings for the first time. And I was disappointed only because I knew I had to wait at least two more years to see this breathtaking, once in a lifetime Sci-Fi-epic come to its spectacular conclusion. Samuel L. Jackson tells a story about seeing "Star Wars" for the first time on opening weekend in 1977. Everyone in the theater was smoking weed, he told "60 Minutes" a couple of years ago, and when the opening titles exploded onto the screen, it blew him back into his seat. He had never seen anything like what George Lucas had created. I saw "Dune" at a press screening in August. No one was smoking weed, everyone wore masks. But when the Hans Zimmer score boomed out of the speakers, I understood what Jackson felt. I had never read "Dune," never even seen the movies. My knowledge of the property was limited to Wikipedia, preview articles, and just general cultural osmosis. But none of that mattered: the movie enveloped me in a way no other Denis Villeneuve work has done prior. I experienced "Dune" inside the recesses of my mind, lost in the wicked sound design and bespoke production. This movie absolutely rules, building to a near anti-climax that basically dares a multi-billion dollar corporation to not make its second part. As much as I want to see how it turns out -- and see how Denis tries to pay off that truly deranged Wiki summary of the book -- I almost hope a sequel doesn't happen. "Dune" deserves to stand as this singular cinematic exhibition. I think Sam Jackson should check it out.
